Kristian Andersen, PhD: The Andersen lab studies how dangerous pathogens emerge, spread, and evolve in human populations, focusing on diseases like SARS-CoV-2, Zika, Ebola, West Nile, and Lassa virus. They combine next-generation genomic sequencing, on-the-ground field work, laboratory experiments, and computational biology to trace outbreaks in real time, often through large international collaborations. A well-known example of this work is their analysis tracing the early spread of COVID-19 to a market in Wuhan, and their research showing mpox had quietly circulated in Nigeria for years before its international outbreak. The goal is to understand the biology of host-pathogen interactions well enough to improve disease surveillance and outbreak response. This lab would suit students interested in genomics, epidemiology, virology, or computational approaches to public health, especially those drawn to fast-moving, collaborative science with real-world stakes.
Ahmed Badran, PhD: The Badran lab uses synthetic biology and protein engineering to tackle environmental and biomedical problems. A major thread of their work is inspired by how plants capture carbon dioxide: they are engineering the photosynthetic enzyme RuBisCO to improve how efficiently plants pull CO2 from the atmosphere, aiming to help offset the effects of fossil fuel use on climate and agriculture. They also develop new molecular biology tools, including methods that expand the genetic code by using four-letter RNA sequences instead of the natural three to build synthetic protein components. Their broader interest is engineering the core molecular machines that make life work, both to discover new medicines and to design climate-relevant biotechnology. Students interested in synthetic biology, protein engineering, or the intersection of chemistry and environmental science would find this lab relevant.
William Balch, PhD: The Balch lab studies how genetic variation across human populations affects the way proteins fold, and how misfolding contributes to disease and aging. They combine experimental techniques from cell biology, biochemistry, and structural biology with computational and machine-learning tools (including Gaussian Process models) to analyze protein structure and function at the level of individual amino acids. A specific focus is the cellular quality-control machinery (chaperone systems like Hsp70 and Hsp90) that manages whether proteins fold correctly. Their work has shown, for example, that some genetic diseases can potentially be corrected not by fixing the mutated gene itself but by controlling how the resulting protein folds. The lab aims to build a general framework for understanding and eventually treating diseases caused by protein misfolding. Good fit for students interested in computational biology, protein science, or genetic disease mechanisms.
Phil Baran, PhD: The Baran lab works in organic chemistry, developing new and more efficient ways to synthesize complex molecules, including natural products and pharmaceuticals. Their central idea is 'ideal synthesis': building complicated molecules in as few steps as possible, avoiding wasteful protective chemistry, and using radical (rather than only classical polar) chemical reactions. They have dramatically shortened the number of steps needed to make certain natural products and have invented widely used chemistry tools, such as reagents for late-stage modification of molecules and a platform for building therapeutic oligonucleotides. The lab also helped popularize modern organic electrochemistry, including co-developing a widely adopted lab device for electrochemical reactions. Their methods are applied across drug discovery, agrochemicals, and materials science. This lab suits students interested in hands-on synthetic organic chemistry with direct applications to medicine and industry.
Donna Blackmond, PhD: The Blackmond lab develops and applies methods for figuring out how chemical reactions actually work at the molecular level. Their signature technique, Reaction Progress Kinetic Analysis (RPKA), uses precise real-time measurements of a reaction as it happens, combined with mathematical analysis, to work out reaction mechanisms from scratch rather than just confirming an existing hypothesis. This approach is used to study important reaction types in pharmaceutical chemistry, including catalytic and asymmetric reactions, and has become a standard tool in industrial drug development. The lab also investigates the origin of 'biological homochirality' — why life uses only one mirror-image form of molecules like amino acids — through kinetic studies and experiments on how chiral molecules behave in solution. Students interested in physical/organic chemistry, reaction mechanisms, or the chemical origins of life would find this lab a good match.
Michael Boddy, PhD: The Boddy lab studies how cells detect and repair damage to their DNA, and how failures in this process contribute to cancer and premature aging. They use a mix of cell biology, proteomics, genetics, and structural biology to understand the molecular machinery involved. A major discovery from the lab was a new family of proteins called STUbLs, which revealed how two cellular tagging systems (SUMO and ubiquitin) work together to manage DNA damage responses, with direct relevance to how certain leukemia therapies work. More recent work has shown that some DNA repair proteins can mimic other cellular signals to hijack these pathways, a finding that connects to both cancer biology and how cells defend against viruses. This lab would appeal to students interested in molecular biology, genome stability, or cancer mechanisms.
Dale L. Boger, PhD: The Boger lab is a synthetic organic chemistry lab focused on designing and building complex molecules with medical applications, especially in the face of rising antibiotic resistance. A major project involves redesigning vancomycin, a critical antibiotic, to create new 'maxamycin' compounds with added mechanisms of action that are more durable against resistant bacteria. The lab has also developed total synthesis routes for natural products like vinblastine, contributed new chemical methods (such as reactions using tetrazine compounds), and worked on treatments for chronic pain and an experimental cancer vaccine. Their broader approach connects fundamental synthetic chemistry with real therapeutic problems. Students interested in medicinal chemistry, drug design, or the chemistry behind fighting antibiotic-resistant infections would find this lab a strong fit.
Michael Bollong, PhD: The Bollong lab works on regenerative medicine, aiming to develop drugs that activate the body's own capacity to repair damaged tissue rather than just manage disease symptoms. They combine traditional drug discovery methods with modern biological techniques to identify and target the molecular pathways that control tissue regeneration. Their research targets a range of conditions including heart disease, inflammatory disease, and fibrosis (scarring) of organs like the lungs. Through Scripps' drug discovery arm, Calibr-Skaggs, the lab's science has advanced to human clinical trials, including an inhaled drug designed to regenerate lung stem cells in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. This lab would interest students drawn to translational medicine, drug discovery, or the biology of tissue repair and regeneration.
Bryan Briney, PhD: The Briney lab studies antibodies, the immune proteins that recognize and fight viruses, with the goal of guiding vaccine design. Their work includes comparing antibody repertoires (the full diversity of antibodies a person or animal can produce) using high-throughput sequencing, and identifying rare, protective antibodies against dangerous viruses like HIV, Lassa, and coronaviruses. By analyzing the structures of antibody-virus complexes across different viral lineages, the lab has helped pinpoint new targets for vaccines and antibody-based therapies. Their research is part of larger collaborative efforts aimed at stockpiling protective antibodies and designing vaccines against future pandemic threats. This lab would suit students interested in immunology, vaccine science, or the genetics of the immune system.
Dennis Burton, PhD: The Burton lab studies broadly neutralizing antibodies — rare immune antibodies capable of fighting off many different strains of highly variable viruses like HIV and coronaviruses. The lab pioneered methods for isolating and characterizing these antibodies, mapping exactly where on a virus's surface they attack, and using that information to guide vaccine design. Their findings have moved from basic antibody discovery through animal testing and into human clinical evaluation, carried out through large NIH- and Gates Foundation-funded research consortia. This work underlies major efforts toward an effective HIV vaccine and informs strategies against influenza and coronaviruses more broadly. Students interested in immunology, virology, or vaccine design, especially the antibody side of the immune response, would find this lab directly relevant.
Sergio Catz, PhD: The Catz lab studies how cells move materials internally through a process called vesicular transport, focusing on a family of proteins called Rab GTPases that organize this trafficking. Using super-resolution microscopy and functional lab assays, they study how vesicular transport controls processes like autophagy, immune cell secretion, and the clearance of pathogens by immune cells such as neutrophils. Their research connects these basic cellular mechanisms to human diseases, including coronary artery disease, lysosomal storage disorders, and autoimmune conditions like lupus. The lab has also built high-throughput screens to discover small-molecule drugs that can adjust vesicular transport, some of which are being tested in preclinical disease models. This lab suits students interested in cell biology, immunology, or drug discovery targeting basic cellular machinery.
Sumit Chanda, PhD: The Chanda lab studies how viruses interact with human cells and how the innate immune system responds, with a particular focus on RNA viruses that carry pandemic risk (such as coronaviruses, influenza, and dengue). Using systems-level and cutting-edge screening approaches, they identify how the body detects and fights these viruses, then use those findings to drive drug discovery through Calibr, Scripps' translational research arm, developing new antivirals, vaccine adjuvants, and immunotherapies. The lab's work is funded by major organizations including the Gates Foundation and NIH, and involves partnerships with pharmaceutical companies. They are also part of the team behind Metascape, a widely used bioinformatics tool for analyzing gene lists. This lab would suit students interested in virology, immunology, or translational antiviral drug discovery.
Michael G. Constantinides, PhD: The Constantinides lab studies how the immune system's 'first responder' cells, called innate lymphocytes, protect barrier tissues like the skin and gut lining, and how they interact with the trillions of microbes (the microbiota) that live there. Their research looks at how microbes shape the development and function of these immune cells, and in turn how the immune cells help regulate the microbial communities, using this two-way relationship to understand immune health. The lab is working to develop targeted approaches to manipulate these interactions as a route toward new therapies for infectious disease, autoimmunity, and cancer. Beyond the science, the lab emphasizes mentorship and expanding access to science for students from underrepresented backgrounds. This lab would suit students interested in immunology, microbiome science, or barrier tissue biology.
Candice Contet, PhD: The Contet lab studies the brain mechanisms behind alcohol's behavioral effects, particularly what drives excessive drinking and the transition to alcohol dependence. One line of research examines specific potassium channels (GIRK and BK) that alcohol activates directly, testing their role in intoxication, tolerance, and chronic drinking using genetically engineered mice. Another line studies brain circuits involving the neuropeptide CRF and a brain region called the parasubthalamic nucleus, which influence motivated behaviors related to alcohol use. The lab also uses untargeted proteomics to search for new molecular contributors to excessive drinking. They combine mouse behavioral models with electrophysiology, mass spectrometry, and bioinformatics, often in collaboration with other labs, aiming ultimately to develop better treatments for alcohol use disorder. Students interested in neuroscience, addiction biology, or behavioral pharmacology would find this lab a strong match.
Benjamin Cravatt, PhD: The Cravatt lab develops chemistry-based technologies to understand what proteins actually do in the body and to find new drug targets. Their signature method, activity-based protein profiling (ABPP), measures whether an enzyme is functionally active in cells and tissues, rather than just how much of it is present, since activity — not abundance — is often what matters for disease. ABPP also serves as a broad platform for discovering small molecules that can bind and control specific proteins, expanding the range of proteins that can be targeted with drugs. Alongside this technology development, the lab studies specific enzymes relevant to the nervous system and cancer, such as FAAH and MAGL, which break down cannabinoid-like signaling molecules. This lab would suit students interested in chemical biology, drug discovery, or neuroscience-related enzymology.
Juan C. De La Torre, PhD: The De La Torre lab studies the molecular and cell biology of mammarenaviruses, a family of viruses that includes lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) and the hemorrhagic-fever-causing Lassa and Junin viruses, which pose serious public health threats. The lab pioneered 'reverse genetics' systems that let researchers rebuild these viruses from cloned DNA, so they can engineer specific mutations and watch exactly how the virus replicates, assembles, and interacts with host cells. Using these tools, the team identifies host proteins the viruses depend on and develops drugs that block those interactions, as well as antivirals that act directly on the virus. They have also engineered weakened versions of LCMV and Lassa virus that protect animals from lethal infection with a single dose, laying groundwork for new live-attenuated vaccines against these dangerous pathogens.
Ashok Deniz, PhD: The Deniz lab investigates the fundamental physics governing proteins, RNA, and other biological molecules, and builds advanced single-molecule tools to study them. A major focus is intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), which lack fixed 3D shapes and instead exist as flexible, shifting structures; the lab's single-molecule experiments reveal how this flexibility relates to function and to diseases like Parkinson's and Alzheimer's. The lab also studies condensates, or membraneless organelles, dynamic droplet-like assemblies of protein, RNA, and other molecules found inside cells (such as the nucleolus and stress granules) that can behave like liquids, gels, or solids and play key roles in cell function. By developing new single-molecule fluorescence methods, the lab directly tests theories about how these structures form and behave, connecting basic biophysics to disease mechanisms.
Christian Diercks, PhD: The Diercks lab uses a system it developed called T7-ORACLE, which drives continuous rapid mutation and evolution in E. coli, to evolve proteins for medicine and synthetic biology faster than conventional lab evolution allows. Current projects include re-engineering the Botox protease to selectively destroy disease-causing proteins as a potential cancer and pain therapy, evolving enzyme replacement therapies for lysosomal storage diseases, improving the specificity of therapeutic antibodies, and creating new tools for expanding the genetic code. The lab is also extending directed evolution beyond biological molecules to engineered nanomaterials, aiming to build non-viral gene-delivery vehicles that more precisely target specific tissues and cell types and escape safely into cells once delivered.
Ilia Droujinine, PhD: The Droujinine lab studies how organs and organisms communicate with each other through proteins secreted into the bloodstream, a poorly understood signaling network relevant to conditions like obesity and diabetes. Because existing tools struggle to detect rare secreted signals and trace where they come from and go, the lab developed a proteomic labeling method (BirA*G3) to track secreted protein trafficking between organs, first in fruit flies and now in engineered mice. Using these approaches, they have identified a fat-tissue-derived protein that regulates muscle activity through a specific receptor, and they investigate how such interorgan signals change during stress, disease, and normal physiology. The lab also explores how secreted proteins from other individuals of a species can influence behavior, expanding beyond known small-molecule pheromone signals.
Cindy Ehlers, PhD: The Ehlers lab studies the genetic and environmental factors that raise or lower a person's risk of developing alcoholism, focusing on Native, African, and Hispanic American populations. The lab examines natural variation in the genes that control alcohol-metabolizing enzymes across ethnic groups and runs genome-wide scans to find other genes linked to alcoholism risk. By combining this genetic data with information on clinical history and environmental risk factors, the team aims to explain how substance dependence develops and to design prevention and treatment programs tailored to different ethnic groups. A second line of research examines how alcohol exposure damages the developing brain in the fetus and during adolescence.
Sandra Encalada, PhD: The Encalada lab studies how neurons transport essential cargo along axons, the long fibers through which brain cells send signals to one another, and what happens when that transport system breaks down. When cellular cargo gets stuck in molecular 'traffic jams,' it can trigger the buildup of toxic protein clumps linked to neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and prion disorders. The lab investigates the cellular pathways underlying this process to understand how these clumps form inside brain cells and to identify ways to block the damage they cause. Their goal is to find new molecules that could treat, or even reverse, complex neurological conditions by restoring healthy transport and preventing toxic aggregation in the brain.
Keary Engle, PhD: The Engle lab develops new catalytic methods for making small organic molecules, which form the basis of most medicines, biological research tools, agrochemicals, and materials, but are often difficult to synthesize with existing chemistry. Conventional routes to these molecules can require many steps, generate significant chemical waste, and demand extensive manual troubleshooting. By harnessing catalysis, the lab aims to make chemical synthesis more efficient, effective, and sustainable. Their projects span synthetic organic, physical organic, and organometallic chemistry, and students in the lab gain interdisciplinary training that extends beyond traditional chemistry boundaries, reflecting the lab's broader goal of rethinking how complex molecules are built.
Michael Erb, PhD: The Erb lab develops 'proximity' drugs, a class of therapeutics that recruit a cell's own protein-disposal machinery to eliminate disease-causing proteins that cannot be targeted by conventional drugs. This approach lets researchers rewire cellular pathways and go after proteins previously considered 'undruggable.' The lab's work has implications for treating breast, prostate, and blood cancers, and their broader research shows how such degrader drugs can be discovered systematically rather than by chance. The team has also studied how small molecules interact with FOXA1, a protein implicated in cancer, identifying a key binding site on its surface that could guide future drug design.
Stefano Forli, PhD: The Forli lab develops and applies computational methods to structural biology and drug design, aiming to rationally design molecules that modulate biological processes. The team combines techniques such as molecular dynamics simulation, homology modeling, and molecular docking to analyze the 3D structures of proteins and other macromolecules and identify sites that could be targeted by drugs. They then screen large virtual libraries of chemical compounds, or design focused libraries based on feasible synthesis routes, to find small molecules that could serve as biological probes or new therapeutics. The lab also builds and freely distributes the widely used AutoDock software suite, which researchers worldwide use to dock small molecules and peptides against proteins and nucleic acids, combining tool-building with active drug discovery.
Martin Friedlander, MD, PhD: The Friedlander lab focuses on treatments for retinal degenerative diseases, particularly a condition called macular telangiectasia (MacTel), which damages central vision. The lab's work contributed to Phase 3 trial results supporting FDA approval of ENCELTO, the first cell-based therapy for a neurodegenerative retinal disease, and they discovered that gene mutations in MacTel patients prevent the eye from making enough of an amino acid needed for eye health. More recent work found that restoring a naturally occurring compound called erucamide in the eye stabilized retinal tissue in preclinical models of degeneration. The lab has also explored using stem cells to counter vision loss, reflecting a long-running effort to find new approaches for treating eye diseases that affect millions of people.
John Griffin, PhD: The Griffin lab studies activated protein C, a natural blood protein, and its role in protecting cells and controlling inflammation. Their research has shown that activated protein C can prevent a type of programmed cell death in blood vessel lining cells by acting through specific cell-surface receptors, revealing a mechanism relevant to cardiovascular disease. Building on this work, the lab has also explored a related drug candidate originally developed to ease inflammation and protect brain cells from damage, and more recent findings point to a potential new application in treating Alzheimer's disease, linking the lab's long-standing work on protein C biology to neurodegeneration research.
Danielle Grotjahn, PhD: The Grotjahn lab studies how mitochondria, the cell's energy-producing structures, change their shape, composition, and function in response to shifting cellular needs and stress. The lab combines cellular cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET), which images cell structures in near-native detail, with super-resolution fluorescence microscopy to connect molecular-level structure to what's happening inside the broader cell. This approach has let them measure things like membrane thickness directly inside intact cells for the first time, and to study processes such as how ribosomes on the mitochondrial surface alter the local environment for protein import. Their goal is to uncover the fundamental mechanisms of mitochondrial adaptation, work that could inform new therapeutic strategies for diseases tied to mitochondrial dysfunction and programmed cell death.
Howard Hang, PhD: The Hang lab studies how chemical signals, called metabolites, mediate interactions between hosts and the microbes living in and on them, particularly in infection and immunity. These metabolites can come from the body's own metabolism or from outside sources like diet, gut microbiota, or drugs, and have historically been hard to study mechanistically. The lab has developed chemical methods to detect how metabolites interact with proteins, and uses animal models to discover protective factors produced by specific gut microbiota species. This work has revealed unexpected ways that metabolites and microbial factors shape immune responses and microbial infection, uncovering new therapeutic leads and biomarkers for infection, inflammation, and immunotherapy, including insights into how gut bacteria communicate with human cells to influence disease and treatment response.
Mia L. Huang, PhD: The Huang Lab studies glycans, the complex sugar molecules that coat and regulate cells, which are hard to analyze because of their structural complexity. The lab wants to understand how glycans direct important biological events like stem cell differentiation, musculoskeletal biology, and cancer, and to build tools that make glycan-protein interactions easier to study. Their approach combines synthetic chemistry, mass spectrometry, and protein engineering. In one line of work, the lab identified galectin-3, a molecule that binds sugars on cell-surface proteins, as key to how placental cells fuse together early in pregnancy; when this process fails, it can cause complications like preeclampsia. The broader goal is to use this chemical-biology toolkit to eventually diagnose or treat conditions such as cancer and liver disease.
Darrell Irvine, PhD: The Irvine Lab engineers new tools to control the immune system, combining immunology with biotechnology and materials chemistry. A major focus is designing synthetic and nanotechnology-based materials that make vaccines work better, particularly for HIV and cancer, and materials that boost the body's own anti-tumor immune responses. The lab collaborates broadly across immunology and microbiology to move discoveries toward real treatments for cancer, infectious disease, and autoimmune conditions. Recent work includes vaccine strategies that generated broadly protective, cross-neutralizing antibodies against HIV in non-human primates, and a DNA-scaffold delivery system that carries HIV vaccine proteins into the body to sharpen immune responses. This matters because effective HIV and cancer vaccines remain major unsolved public health challenges.
Kim Janda, PhD: The Janda Lab develops vaccines and antibody-based treatments that train the immune system to neutralize dangerous drugs before they can harm the body. Their work targets synthetic opioids like fentanyl, its emerging analogs, and carfentanil (which is far more potent than fentanyl), as well as xylazine, aiming to prevent or reverse overdoses. One approach involves an early-stage vaccine against xylazine overdose, while other projects developed a human antibody that reverses carfentanil and fentanyl overdose effects, and a modified opioid molecule that blocks pain while causing less of the respiratory depression that kills overdose victims. This research matters directly for the ongoing opioid overdose crisis, offering potential new medical tools beyond current treatments.
Jeffery Kelly, PhD: The Kelly Lab studies protein folding and what happens when proteins misfold or clump together, since this underlies diseases like Alzheimer's and amyloid disorders (including transthyretin- and light-chain-based amyloidosis). Using chemistry, biophysics, and biology together, the lab designs small molecules that stabilize proteins or block harmful aggregation; this work led to the drug tafamidis, now sold by Pfizer. They also run cell-based screens to find molecules that boost the cell's natural protein-quality-control systems, including stress-response pathways and autophagy, and study lysosomal storage diseases by seeking small molecules that help misfolded enzymes fold and traffic correctly. Separately, with the Wong lab, they discovered glycan-protein interactions that stabilize proteins, informing new synthetic and medicinal chemistry strategies for proteostasis-targeted drugs.
Megan Ken, MD, PhD: The Ken Lab studies how RNA molecules fold, move, and interact with proteins, using HIV as a key model system. A central project models how the HIV genome's RNA "leader" region interacts with the Gag protein to package new virus particles, using high-throughput mutation experiments that measure how thousands of RNA variants behave in test tubes and in cells. More broadly, the lab combines computational modeling with experiments (including NMR) to understand RNA structure and dynamics, aiming to identify rare, non-functional RNA shapes that could be targeted by small-molecule drugs. This matters because RNA is a promising but difficult drug target, and better quantitative models could open new paths to antiviral and other RNA-targeted therapies.
Ann Kennedy, PhD: The Kennedy Lab studies how the brain learns, makes decisions, and pursues goals, focusing on fear, survival, and social behavior. They examine how populations of neurons represent sensory and internal information across brain regions including the hypothalamus (social and defensive behavior), basal ganglia (behavior control), and hippocampus (social bonding). Their approach draws on dynamical systems theory, statistical modeling, and machine learning to analyze neural activity data. The goal is to uncover general principles of flexible, adaptive behavior and to understand what goes wrong in dysfunction, such as excessive fear, anxiety, or social impairment. This matters for understanding both normal brain function and psychiatric or neurological conditions rooted in disrupted decision-making and social circuits.
Dorothee Kern, PhD: The Kern Lab studies how proteins move, not just their static structures. While tools like AlphaFold give snapshots of protein shape, biological function actually depends on proteins constantly shifting between different conformations, what the lab calls the "dance of proteins." They combine experimental methods, including NMR, x-ray crystallography, cryo-EM, and fluorescence spectroscopy, with computational approaches like molecular dynamics simulations and ancestral sequence reconstruction (recreating ancient proteins in the lab) to map this motion at atomic resolution. This has revealed how protein dynamics drive enzyme activity, cell signaling, drug transport, and immune cell maturation. Practically, they apply lessons from protein evolution to design better enzymes and drugs, including green biocatalysts developed through directed evolution combined with machine learning.
Luke Lairson, PhD: The Lairson Lab studies the body's natural repair pathways in the brain and nervous system, with a focus on multiple sclerosis (MS), an autoimmune disease where the immune system attacks myelin, the protective coating around neurons. Their research investigates how to activate the body's own stem cells to rebuild damaged myelin, aiming to develop therapies that go beyond current treatments, which cannot fully repair MS damage, and instead halt disease progression. The lab's broader chemistry-driven drug discovery work includes turning simple chemical building blocks into complex, nature-like 3-D structures, and identifying compounds that can restore exhausted T cells in cancerous tumors so the immune system can better fight cancer.
Katja Lamia, PhD: The Lamia Lab studies circadian rhythms, the roughly 24-hour internal clocks that let the body track time of day and adjust its physiology accordingly, and what happens when these rhythms are disrupted. Their research connects circadian disruption, such as long-term shift work, to increased cancer risk, and has identified a family of temperature-responsive genes with unexpected roles in cancer. The lab's work also touches on metabolism, showing that some long-held ideas about metabolic disorders, weight control, and eating habits are being revised, with implications for new drug development. This matters because understanding the molecular links between the body's internal clock, metabolism, and disease could open new treatment strategies for cancer and metabolic conditions.
Gabriel Lander, PhD: The Lander Lab develops advanced cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) methods, improving sample preparation, data collection, and image-processing algorithms to see molecular structures at higher resolution. They combine these imaging techniques with biochemical and cellular studies to understand protein degradation, the process cells use to break down and recycle unwanted or damaged proteins, which is essential for cellular balance. This involves visualizing large molecular machines and motors as they undergo shape changes to select, unfold, and eliminate target proteins. The lab also studies small molecules that can modulate these degradation systems for potential therapeutic benefit. This work has implications for diseases linked to breakdowns in cellular quality control, including cancer, heart disease, and neurodegeneration.
Keren Lasker, PhD: The Lasker Lab studies biomolecular condensates, membraneless compartments that cells use to organize their chemistry through a process called phase separation. Using PopZ, a protein found in certain bacteria, as a model system, they study how condensates assemble, adjust their physical properties, and select which proteins to interact with. The lab combines cryo-electron tomography, high-resolution live-cell imaging, quantitative biophysics, and computational modeling to link condensate structure to cellular function, such as organizing cell division. They are now engineering synthetic condensates in human cells that can capture specific target proteins and route them for degradation, with a focus on disease-associated proteins that misfold or accumulate in neurodegenerative and age-related disorders.
Mansun Law, PhD: The Law Lab studies viral hepatitis, especially hepatitis B (HBV) and hepatitis C (HCV) viruses, with the goal of contributing to their eventual eradication. Their research investigates the virology and immunology of chronic infection, including how antibodies and B cells (immune cells that produce antibodies) respond to these viruses, and applies this understanding to vaccine design. In experiments, mice given virus-mimicking particles produced stronger antibody responses than mice given hepatitis C proteins alone, suggesting a promising vaccine strategy. This work matters because HBV and HCV cause chronic liver infections affecting millions of people worldwide and can lead to liver failure and cancer, and effective vaccines could help eliminate this disease burden.
Amy Lightner, MD: The Lightner lab studies inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), including ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease, conditions that affect about 1 in 100 people in the US and lack curative treatments. Dr. Lightner, a colorectal surgeon and scientist, uses organoids grown from tissue taken from her own surgical patients to model IBD in the lab and search for the causes of the disease. Her lab uses these organoid models to discover potential new therapies focused on regenerating and restoring damaged intestinal tissue, rather than just easing symptoms. Promising treatments developed this way are then advanced into first-in-human clinical trials, including work on regenerative, tissue-repairing drug candidates for IBD. The lab's approach bridges the operating room and the bench, aiming to both better understand what causes IBD and deliver more effective treatments to patients who currently have few good options.
Giordano Lippi, PhD: The Lippi lab studies how neurons control where and when genes are turned into proteins, since neurons must manage protein production separately in distant regions like the axon and dendrites, and also undergo big gene-expression changes as they develop. The lab focuses especially on microRNAs, small non-coding RNA molecules that fine-tune gene expression and are enriched in the brain. Using techniques including single-unit recording in freely moving animals, calcium imaging, electrophysiology, and behavioral studies, the lab has shown that briefly blocking specific microRNAs can permanently disrupt neural circuits, causing excessive synaptic activity, seizure-like activity, and memory problems. By identifying the molecular pathways these microRNAs control, the lab aims to understand how properly balanced neural networks are built during development, work that connects to neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism, schizophrenia, and epilepsy.
Tiantian Liu: The Liu lab studies the gene regulatory networks that control how Antigen-Presenting Cells develop. These immune cells play a central role in activating and directing T cell responses, and the lab uses genetically engineered mouse models to understand what makes each subset of Antigen-Presenting Cell unique versus overlapping in function. The long-term goal is to apply these insights toward designing new vaccines and immune therapies that can better modulate T cell responses, with potential applications in infectious disease, autoimmune disorders, and cancer.
Yuzhong Liu, PhD: The Liu lab uses synthetic biology and biocatalysis to produce and diversify complex, biologically active natural molecules that are normally hard or environmentally costly to obtain. A major focus is QS-21, a rare vaccine adjuvant (a molecule that boosts vaccine effectiveness) traditionally harvested from soapbark trees in a damaging, labor-intensive process; the lab engineered yeast to produce it instead. By combining pathway engineering, enzyme discovery and evolution, microbial fermentation, and chemical biology, the lab studies complex sugar-containing molecules (glycosides) and how sugar structures affect a compound's behavior in the body and its ability to activate the immune system. The broader goal is to use natural and engineered enzymes as programmable tools for chemical synthesis, enabling new vaccine adjuvants, cancer therapies, and other medicines.
Ian MacRae, PhD: The MacRae lab studies the molecular mechanisms behind RNA interference (RNAi), a natural gene-silencing process important for viral defense, development, stem cell division, and memory. The lab combines structural biology with biochemistry and cell biology to understand RISC (RNA-Induced Silencing Complexes), the molecular machines that silence genes by degrading or blocking specific messenger RNAs. A particular focus is the RISC-loading complex, which determines what RNA sequence gets targeted for silencing. The lab has captured high-resolution structural images of the human protein Argonaute 2, revealing why some small interfering RNA (siRNA) molecules work better than others. This structural knowledge is aimed at guiding the design of more effective RNAi-based therapeutics for human disease.
Anton Maximov, PhD: The Maximov lab studies how the brain forms and stores memories by investigating how neurons connect to each other at the molecular, cellular, and circuit level. The lab focuses on the hippocampus, a brain region central to memory, emotion, and navigation, using genetic, biophysical, and behavioral techniques along with optical imaging, serial electron microscopy, and computational tools. A key question is how networks of excitatory and inhibitory neurons reorganize during learning, and how this rewiring underlies memory formation. The lab also combines human genetics data, unbiased genetic screens, and mouse models to identify the molecular basis of this network plasticity, and designs new tools to precisely manipulate specific neural circuits. This work has helped reveal structural features of long-term memory (engrams) and has implications for treating memory loss and neurodegenerative disease.
Alejandra Mendoza, PhD: The Mendoza lab studies how the nervous system and immune system communicate at barrier tissues (like skin and gut) that interface with the environment, to sense and respond to things like heat, injury, chemical stress, and infection. One focus is how sensory neurons influence inflammation, including how the body's own opioid-like signaling molecules mediate communication between neurons and immune cells to regulate pain, itch, and tissue balance. Another focus is how environmental signals shape the activation states of immune cells at these barrier sites, giving rise to distinct effector, memory, and regulatory immune cell populations. The lab aims to map the spatial organization and function of these immune circuits, with implications for understanding chronic inflammation, infection response, tumor growth, and how the body decides whether to attack or tolerate a given stimulus.
David Millar, PhD: The Millar lab studies the dynamic structural changes that occur during DNA processing and RNA catalysis using biophysical chemistry techniques. One project examines how DNA polymerases proofread themselves during DNA replication, using time-resolved and single-molecule fluorescence methods combined with site-directed mutagenesis to track how a DNA strand moves between the enzyme's copying site and its separate error-correcting (exonuclease) site. The lab uses similar fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) methods to watch the hairpin ribozyme, a small catalytic RNA, fold into its active shape in real time, and to study Holliday junctions, four-stranded DNA structures formed during genetic recombination and DNA repair.
Shannon Miller, PhD: The Miller lab develops and applies gene-editing technologies for treating genetic disease, working to overcome current limitations like toxicity, limited editing capabilities, and difficulty delivering editing tools into the body. Research spans protein engineering, directed evolution, and both viral and non-viral delivery methods. Three major areas of focus are: engineering improved AAV viral vectors for delivering gene therapies and for industrial-scale production; developing new methods for making large-scale DNA edits; and improving CRISPR-based therapies in living organisms using chemically modified guide RNAs. The lab's past work includes using base editing to correct sickle cell disease in mice and developing new Cas9 variants with broader targeting capabilities, aiming toward safer, more effective one-time genetic cures.
Marco Mravic, PhD: The Mravic lab uses protein design and computational modeling to study how proteins are structured and function within cell membranes, a challenging environment to study directly. The lab has three main focuses: designing small synthetic membrane proteins as simplified model systems to test basic questions about molecular structure and function; creating custom chemical tools that target membrane proteins at their lipid-embedded regions to probe how they work and identify potential therapeutic targets; and using molecular modeling and dynamics simulations, integrated with experimental data, to understand key molecular events at cell membranes. The lab combines protein chemical synthesis, structural biology methods (X-ray, NMR, cryo-EM), cell-based assays, bioinformatics, and machine learning to establish general chemical rules governing membrane protein structure, aiming to better understand molecular mechanisms of disease.
Arthur Olson, PhD: The Olson lab develops computational and visualization techniques for studying how biomolecules like proteins and nucleic acids interact with each other, applying these tools to drug design and understanding protein assemblies. The lab created AutoDock and AutoDock Vina, widely used software (by tens of thousands of researchers worldwide) that predicts how small molecules dock into protein binding sites, aiding the design of new drugs and inhibitors, including for anti-HIV therapeutics. The lab also builds mesoscale computational models of entire cellular environments containing millions of individual biomolecules, and uses 3D printing and augmented reality to create new ways of visualizing and interacting with molecular structures for research and education. Their distributed computing project FightAIDS@Home has run on over 2 million volunteer computers to help find HIV drug candidates.
Donghyun Raphael Park, PhD: The Park lab studies how disease-causing bacteria use complex molecular machines to inject harmful proteins into host cells, a key step in infection. Using cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET), an advanced imaging technique, the lab aims to visualize how these bacterial nanomachines assemble and function within their natural cellular environment, revealing how they enable pathogens to hijack host cell processes and cause disease. This structural understanding of host-pathogen interactions is aimed at informing future strategies against bacterial infections, including antibiotic-resistant strains.
Christopher Parker, PhD: The Parker Lab uses chemistry to study human biology and disease. They combine organic synthesis (building new molecules) with chemical proteomics (mapping how molecules interact with proteins) and cell/molecular biology. One goal is understanding how small molecules can regulate complex biological processes like immune responses; another is figuring out the molecular mechanisms behind disease. Their work has included developing inhibitors of a protein involved in inflammation and lupus, and creating new high-resolution techniques for finding druggable sites on proteins inside living cells. Beyond basic understanding, the lab aims to build chemical tools and technologies that could become starting points for new therapeutics, and members have gone on to found biotech companies based on this research.
Ardem Patapoutian, PhD: The Patapoutian Lab studies mechanotransduction — how cells sense physical force, which underlies touch, pain, hearing, and blood pressure regulation, and had been poorly understood at the molecular level. The lab discovered PIEZO1 and PIEZO2, ion channels that open in response to mechanical force. Genetic studies from the lab showed PIEZO2 is the key sensor for touch, body position, and blood pressure sensing in vessels, while PIEZO1 senses blood flow and affects vascular development. They've since identified other mechanosensors (GPR68, OSCA/TMEM63 family) and continue searching for new ones. Ongoing work asks how these channels and receptors function in the body, connecting basic molecular discovery to conditions involving sensory disorders and cardiovascular regulation.
Michael Petrascheck, PhD: The Petrascheck Lab studies aging and how it drives disease and mortality. Because certain genetic pathways can be manipulated to extend lifespan, the lab screens for small molecules that extend lifespan in simple model organisms (C. elegans roundworms) and mice. Small molecules are useful because they can be tested across cell lines, multiple species, disease models, and combined with genetic mutations affecting aging. By using these lifespan-extending compounds as research tools, the lab investigates the molecular links between aging and age-related diseases — for example, showing that the antibiotic minocycline extends worm lifespan by preventing harmful protein buildup. The broader goal is finding treatments that target aging pathways themselves rather than individual diseases.
Lisa Racki, PhD: The Racki Lab studies how bacteria survive periods of starvation, which is common both in nature and during chronic infections in the human body. Most antibiotics target processes active during bacterial growth, like DNA replication or cell wall building, but are far less effective against starved, slow-growing bacteria. The lab investigates how bacteria reorganize their internal subcellular structure to endure these conditions. Their research has revealed how long phosphate-chain molecules (polyphosphates) interact with DNA and magnesium to help bacteria slow down internal movement and enter a dormant, antibiotic-evading state. Understanding this mechanism could point toward new ways to target slow-growing, hard-to-treat bacterial infections, such as those in the lungs, blood, or on medical devices.
Chen Ran, PhD: The Ran Lab studies 'internal senses' — how the brain interprets signals from inside the body, such as hunger, fullness, thirst, nausea, low oxygen, and internal pain, and why similar stimuli (like stomach vs. bladder stretch) produce very different sensations. To study this, the lab built a novel two-photon brain imaging system that records activity from thousands of individual neurons in the brainstem, the brain region that receives signals from internal organs, while researchers deliver controlled stimuli to those organs. This revealed that internal organs are mapped onto the brainstem in an organized way, a 'visceral homunculus.' Combining imaging, electrophysiology, genetics, and neural circuit manipulation, the lab aims to uncover principles that could inform treatments for conditions like obesity, hypertension, and nausea.
Marisa Roberto, PhD: The Roberto Lab studies Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) and addiction to other drugs, aiming to understand the brain changes that drive dependence, since current treatments remain limited. The lab focuses on synapses — the connections between neurons — particularly in the central nucleus of the amygdala, a brain region central to both drug responses and stress/fear reactions. Using electrophysiology, pharmacology, and molecular methods, they've identified how alcohol alters GABA and glutamate signaling, and found that the drug gabapentin can reverse some effects of alcohol dependence in animal studies. The lab also studies stress-related neuropeptides (like CRF, oxytocin, neuropeptide Y) and other systems (endocannabinoids, opioids, immune signaling) to understand 'reward' versus 'relief' drinking, working toward new addiction therapies.
Edward Roberts, PhD: The Roberts Lab is involved in discovering and developing drugs that target the sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P) receptor system, work that contributed to ozanimod, a therapy approved for multiple sclerosis and ulcerative colitis and in development for Crohn's disease. Roberts co-invented ozanimod alongside colleague Hugh Rosen. Published work from the lab includes a patent review of S1P receptor 1 agonist compounds. Beyond this, the provided material is largely news coverage of drug approvals rather than a detailed description of the lab's current research questions or methods, so specifics about ongoing projects are limited.
Hugh Rosen, MD, PhD: The Rosen Lab, led by a physician-scientist, develops new medicines by targeting specific molecular pathways in disease. The lab co-invented ozanimod, an approved treatment for multiple sclerosis and ulcerative colitis, and navacaprant, a compound now in Phase 3 trials for major depressive disorder that targets a specific brain circuit. More recent work from the lab has produced first-in-class molecules that block a particular protein interaction in immune cells, aiming to reduce inflammation in autoimmune diseases like lupus and rheumatoid arthritis without broadly suppressing immunity. Overall, the lab's approach centers on translating molecular-level drug discovery into precisely targeted therapies for immune and neuropsychiatric disease.
Enrique Saez, PhD: The Saez Lab studies how the body regulates energy balance, focusing on two areas. First, nuclear receptors — proteins that sense dietary components like lipids, vitamins, and cholesterol derivatives and control gene expression in response. The lab uses high-throughput cell-based and biochemical screens plus animal models to find new nutrient-sensing pathways involving these receptors. Second, the genetic regulation of energy storage in fat (adipose) tissue: the lab uses genomic and chemical approaches to identify genes that control fat tissue formation and their role in metabolic disease. The overall goal is understanding how diet influences gene expression and energy storage, in order to identify new therapeutic targets for obesity and diabetes.
William Schief, PhD: The Schief Lab designs vaccines, with a major focus on HIV, using a strategy called germline-targeting: engineering immunogens that can prime specific types of immune cells to eventually produce antibodies capable of neutralizing many HIV strains. The lab also works on protein design, nanoparticle vaccine platforms, mRNA vaccines and therapeutics, and studies of antibody structure and how antibodies recognize viral proteins. Their germline-targeting approach has advanced through preclinical studies and into clinical trials in North America and Africa, showing proof-of-concept for training the immune system toward broadly neutralizing antibodies. The lab has also applied similar universal-vaccine strategies to influenza and coronavirus, aiming for vaccines effective against many variants of a virus.
Peter Schultz, PhD: The Schultz Lab works at the interface of chemistry and biology, notably pioneering methods to expand the genetic code — adding new, non-natural chemical building blocks (amino acids) that cells can incorporate into proteins. This includes tools like genetically encoded 'photocaged' amino acids, which let researchers control protein activity, such as phosphorylation, using light. More broadly, Schultz's research and institutional leadership emphasize combining basic chemical biology discovery with translational drug development, spanning areas like protein evolution platforms, enzyme engineering, and new therapeutic approaches for cancer, infectious disease, and regenerative medicine. The lab's chemistry-driven tools are aimed at both answering fundamental biological questions and creating starting points for new diagnostics and treatments.
Ian B. Seiple, PhD: The Seiple Lab develops new antibiotics using chemical synthesis to fight drug-resistant bacterial infections. Many natural antibiotics come from microbial competition but aren't optimized for human use and provoke resistance; the lab builds fully synthetic, modular routes to recreate and improve natural product scaffolds, focusing on two classes of protein-synthesis-blocking antibiotics (streptogramins and lankacidins), and uses cryo-EM with collaborators to see exactly how these compounds act on bacterial ribosomes. Because most antibiotics don't work against Gram-negative bacteria, the lab is also engineering ways to convert Gram-positive antibiotics into Gram-negative-active ones by exploiting bacterial periplasm enzymes. Separate collaborations apply antibody-based approaches to targeted protein degradation and CRISPR-based high-throughput screening for new antibiotics.
K. Barry Sharpless, PhD: Sharpless is best known for developing 'click chemistry,' a highly efficient, reliable approach for snapping together molecular building blocks, which won him a share of the 2022 Nobel Prize in Chemistry — his second, after his 2001 Nobel for chirally catalyzed oxidation reactions. Click chemistry and its related bioorthogonal chemistry make it easier to construct complex molecules for uses spanning drug discovery, polymer science, and materials science, including environmentally friendlier ways to generate large libraries of new compounds. The provided material centers on these landmark chemistry methods and their applications rather than describing current specific lab projects in detail.
Ryan Shenvi, PhD: The Shenvi lab studies chemical synthesis, focusing on complex "information-dense" molecules like natural products that are hard to make with existing tools. They develop new synthetic and computational methods (including density functional theory and neural network potentials) to predict how reactions will behave before running them in the lab, turning a handful of experiments into large sets of predicted outcomes and saving wet-lab time. They apply these tools to biomedical targets, notably kappa-opioid receptor ligands (salvinorin A, GB18) developed into selective, G protein-biased agonists, plus programs on 14-3-3 protein-client molecular glues, GABAa receptor antagonists, and species-selective SDH inhibitors. Their work aims to unlock faster routes to the branched, complex molecular frameworks found in drugs and materials, bridging fundamental chemistry with pharmaceutical discovery.
Supriya Srinivasan, PhD: The Srinivasan lab studies the gut-brain axis as a key regulator of metabolism, using the roundworm C. elegans as a genetically tractable model. They investigate how neuroendocrine and enteroendocrine signals let the intestine and nervous system communicate to control energy balance, feeding behavior, fat metabolism, and lifespan, focusing on how animals sense their internal state and respond via GPCRs, neuropeptides, and insulin-like signaling. Using large-scale genetic and small-molecule screens enabled by C. elegans's well-mapped neural circuitry, they uncover conserved molecular mechanisms. The lab has also extended into mammalian intestinal biology, examining how gut-derived signals affect fat mobilization, mucosal immunity, and inflammation—work relevant to obesity, type 2 diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease, and healthy aging.
Lisa Stowers Anderson, PhD: The Stowers lab is a neuroscience group studying how the brain detects and interprets odors and pheromones and turns them into behavior. Past work has shown that a specialized sensory organ (the vomeronasal organ) detects protein pheromone-like molecules to trigger defensive behavior between species, that urinary proteins involved in scent communication evolved differently across species, and that male pheromones can influence female reproductive development. More recent work aims to map a complete neural circuit in the mammalian brain connecting odor detection to behavior, and touches on interoception—how the brain senses signals from internal organs like the heart and stomach. Overall, the lab combines molecular, genetic, and circuit-level approaches to understand how the nervous system processes chemical and internal-body signals.
Andrew Su, PhD: The Su lab is a bioinformatics group that builds computational tools to organize and connect biomedical knowledge at scale. They develop widely used resources like the BioThings suite (MyGene.info, MyVariant.info, MyChem.info) and contribute to large knowledge graphs such as the NCATS Biomedical Data Translator, integrating data from hundreds of sources. Using statistics, computer science, and AI, they mine these datasets to generate testable hypotheses—for example identifying drug-repurposing opportunities and mapping drug mechanisms via their DrugMechDB resource. They collaborate with experimental scientists on single-cell transcriptomics, circadian biology, and infectious disease, and are increasingly exploring how AI agents and large language models can help scientists generate ideas and synthesize literature, with an emphasis on open, transparent, and reliable tools.
John Teijaro, PhD: The Teijaro lab studies viral immunology, using LCMV to model persistent viral infection and influenza virus to study acute viral disease in mice. They investigate how type 1 interferon signaling drives both the initiation/maintenance of persistent infection and the harmful cytokine amplification and immune pathology seen in influenza. Key findings include that endothelial (not epithelial) cells are central to cytokine amplification during flu infection, that blocking this amplification improves survival, and that blocking type 1 interferon signaling during persistent LCMV infection speeds viral clearance in a CD4 T cell-dependent way while restoring immune tissue structure. The lab also has a history studying memory CD4 T cells and tissue-resident immunity following influenza infection.
Luc Teyton, MD, PhD: The Teyton lab pursues two main lines of research. First, in response to rising antibiotic resistance, they develop therapeutic antibodies against bacterial and fungal glycans (surface sugar structures), using synthetic conjugate immunogens to generate high-affinity antibodies; this approach has shown proof-of-concept efficacy against Streptococcus pneumoniae and antibiotic-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, guided by structural and synthetic chemistry studies. Second, for over 25 years they have studied how the immune system destroys insulin-producing beta cells in type 1 diabetes, examining the normal relationship between the endocrine pancreas and immune system and how it breaks down. This work spans mice and humans, using modern genetics, immunology, stem-cell-derived islet organoids, and single-cell analysis, aiming toward clinical trials for prevention and treatment.
Eric Topol, MD: Eric Topol leads a research program at Scripps Research focused on translational and digital medicine. A practicing cardiologist, he directs the Scripps Research Translational Institute and is principal investigator on NIH grants supporting innovations to promote human health. His work explores how artificial intelligence can be applied to healthcare, including self-supervised learning methods in medicine, and he has written extensively on AI's role in making healthcare more human. His group is currently running a digital clinical trial testing a repurposed GIP/GLP-1 dual receptor agonist (already approved for type 2 diabetes, obesity, and sleep apnea) for relief of long COVID symptoms, reflecting a broader focus on applying data-driven and AI-based approaches to real-world clinical problems.
Ali Torkamani, PhD: The Torkamani lab uses genomic and informatic technologies to identify the genetic causes and mechanisms behind human disease, aiming to define individual health risks and personalized interventions. Major focus areas include interpreting the human genome, discovering the genetics behind novel rare diseases, and building machine- and deep-learning models that predict risk for common diseases like coronary artery disease and pre-diabetes using genetic and wearable-sensor data. The lab also works on communicating genetically-informed disease risk to patients digitally. Their tools are being integrated into remote clinical trials that deliver personalized behavioral and therapeutic interventions, with the broader goal of using genomic data to help restore individuals to their personal baseline of health.
Renan V.H. de Carvalho, PhD: The Laboratory of Immune Longevity (LIL), led by Renan de Carvalho, studies what makes immune responses last a long time. Their top priority is understanding plasma cell longevity and what determines durable antibody (humoral) immunity—identifying why some immune responses produce lasting protection while others don't. Using transgenic mouse models combined with infection and immunization strategies, the lab investigates the underlying mechanisms of successful long-lived immunity. De Carvalho's prior work includes studies on immune evasion by Leishmania parasites and on how germinal centers (the sites where antibody-producing cells mature) are sustained after respiratory virus infection, giving the lab a background spanning infectious disease immunology and vaccine-relevant immune memory.
Julia Moore Vogel, PhD: The Moore Vogel lab conducts participant-centric health research and clinical trials aimed at complex, poorly understood illnesses, with a particular focus on long COVID. Rather than traditional in-clinic studies, they run decentralized trials using digital technologies, wearable sensors, and at-home biospecimen collection so people across the country and world can participate. As senior director of the All of Us Research Program, Julia Moore Vogel—who also lives with long COVID—directs research toward better symptom management and health equity for affected patients. One current study is testing a repurposed GIP/GLP-1 dual receptor agonist (approved for type 2 diabetes, obesity, and sleep apnea) for relief of long COVID symptoms.
Andrew Ward, PhD: The Ward lab uses integrative structural biology to study membrane proteins and viruses. They investigate membrane protein transporters, which move molecules into and out of cells, using x-ray crystallography, electron microscopy, and other biophysical techniques to uncover their largely unknown molecular mechanisms. A major focus is on viral surface proteins that mediate cell entry and how broadly neutralizing antibodies bind to and block viruses like HIV and influenza; using single-particle electron microscopy and electron tomography, they visualize antibody-virus complexes and whole viruses to understand how these antibodies work and to help design better vaccine immunogens capable of eliciting similar broad protection in humans.
Friedbert Weiss, PhD: The Weiss lab studies the neurobiology of drug and alcohol addiction, focusing on the brain circuits underlying motivation, reinforcement, and reward. Their research examines the neuropharmacology, neurocircuitry, and molecular basis of addiction, including how dependence and withdrawal develop, what drives drug craving and relapse, and how addiction impairs memory and cognitive function. Notable findings include identifying that cues associated with a single cocaine experience can trigger long-lasting drug-seeking behavior, and that the brain learns to seek alcohol for relief rather than just pleasure. Using animal models, the lab's work aims to inform better treatments for reducing cravings and relapse in people with substance use and alcohol use disorders.
James Williamson, PhD: The Williamson lab studies the structural biology of RNA and RNA-protein complexes. A core focus is ribosome assembly: using isotope pulse-chase mass spectrometry, single-molecule fluorescence, and time-resolved electron microscopy (with several collaborators), they measure the kinetics and cooperativity of ribosomal protein binding both in vitro and inside cells. They also study how RNA folds into 3D structures and is recognized by proteins, how RNA-binding proteins regulate stem cell differentiation in C. elegans germline development using x-ray crystallography, and how RNA-binding proteins control T-cell activation. Another line of work examines helicases involved in HIV replication, using biochemical and crystallographic methods to understand their role in transporting viral mRNA within infected cells.
Ian Wilson, PhD: The Wilson lab uses high-resolution x-ray crystal structures to understand how the immune system recognizes and neutralizes pathogens, aiming to inform vaccine design. They have solved over 250 structures of antibodies bound to diverse antigens, plus structures of T-cell receptors with MHC molecules and pattern-recognition receptors like Toll-like receptors, revealing how the immune system detects microbial threats. Much recent work focuses on HIV-1 and influenza: the lab has determined structures of rare broadly neutralizing antibodies against HIV-1's envelope proteins and against influenza hemagglutinin, identifying vulnerable sites on the viruses that can guide vaccine development, including for the 1918 flu strain and avian/swine influenza variants with pandemic potential.
R. Luke Wiseman, PhD: The Wiseman lab studies how cells sense and respond to stress. Every cell has built-in signaling pathways that detect damage from genetics, environment, or aging, then trigger changes that protect the cell. The lab focuses on pathways controlling protein homeostasis — how cells keep their proteins properly folded and functioning — including the unfolded protein response, integrated stress response, and heat shock response. When these pathways break down, misfolded or toxic proteins can build up, contributing to diseases like neurodegeneration, metabolic disorders, cardiovascular disease, and inflammation. By working out exactly how these stress pathways protect cells, the lab aims to find ways to therapeutically "hijack" the body's own defenses — developing single drugs that could potentially treat multiple, seemingly unrelated diseases by restoring healthy protein balance.
Chi-Huey Wong, PhD: The Wong lab works at the intersection of chemistry and biology, focused on glycosylation — the sugar molecules attached to proteins that shape how those proteins behave. They develop new chemical and enzymatic methods to build complex sugar chains (oligosaccharides) and glycoproteins, along with tools like glycan microarrays and glycoengineered antibodies, to study how sugars influence cancer growth, bacterial and viral infection, neurodegenerative disease, and immune responses. The goal is to find carbohydrate-related drug targets and use them to design next-generation medicines, including low-sugar cancer/microbial vaccines and antibodies engineered for better immune effectiveness. The lab also combines its wet-lab data with AI approaches to accelerate discovery of these sugar-based therapies.
Peter Wright, PhD: The Wright lab uses nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and other biophysical methods to study how proteins are shaped, how they move, and how they fold — information that's hard to get with other techniques since NMR can capture proteins in motion, not just frozen structures. One major focus is intrinsically disordered proteins, which lack a fixed shape but are crucial to cell signaling; the lab studies proteins like CBP/p300 and the tumor suppressor p53 to understand how these flexible proteins fold only once they bind their targets. Another focus is protein misfolding diseases: they use NMR to watch how the protein transthyretin unfolds and clumps together, a process that leads to amyloid disease. Overall, the lab aims to reveal the hidden, fleeting structural states that control how proteins function or malfunction.
Peng Wu, PhD: The Wu lab combines synthetic chemistry with glycobiology (the study of sugar molecules on cells) to understand how immune cells recognize and respond to cancer and infections. A major theme is figuring out which T cells are specifically reacting to a threat versus just "bystanders" caught up in the response, since chronic stimulation can cause T cells to become dysfunctional. The lab designs new chemical tools to detect and separate these T-cell populations, aiming to improve therapies that boost antigen-specific T cells' persistence against infection and cancer. They also study Siglecs, immune receptors that bind sugar molecules on tumor cells and can suppress anti-tumor immunity; using a chemistry technique called SuFEx click chemistry, they're building synthetic molecules to block this interaction and potentially unleash stronger immune responses against tumors.
Kurt Wuthrich, PhD: The Wuthrich group has spent decades pioneering the use of nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy to determine the 3D structures of large biological molecules in solution, including developing the TROSY technique that made NMR usable on very large molecular complexes. Research has spanned differentiation in higher organisms, immune suppression, and neuropathology. More recently, work at Scripps Research and ETH Zurich has centered on healthy aging, particularly how sarcopenia (age-related muscle loss) affects human healthspan, while a parallel effort at ShanghaiTech University uses NMR to study how G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) transmit signals across cell membranes.
John Yates, PhD: The Yates lab develops tools and strategies in proteomics — the large-scale study of proteins — building on the wealth of genomic sequence data now available. They combine peptide tandem mass spectrometry (which reveals amino acid sequence information) with database searching and advanced separation techniques to directly analyze extremely complex mixtures of proteins, something that was previously very difficult. This approach lets them study everything from purified protein complexes to how pathogens like malaria and anthrax interact with their hosts. The lab is also extending these methods to detect post-translational modifications — chemical changes to proteins after they're made — within these same complex samples, helping answer fundamental questions in biology and disease.
Li Ye, PhD: The Ye lab studies how the brain senses and adapts to the body's metabolic state — and how that adaptation, in turn, shapes whole-body physiology. Because neurons demand so much energy, the brain is especially sensitive to metabolic stress, whether short-term or chronic. The lab investigates this at the molecular, cellular, and circuit level, with a long-term goal of targeting metabolic disorders like obesity and type 2 diabetes, as well as related neurodegenerative diseases. To do this, they build and apply cutting-edge tools: whole-brain imaging techniques (tissue-clearing methods like CLARITY/HYBRiD paired with light-sheet microscopy), simultaneous calcium imaging across multiple brain regions, optogenetics tied to specific circuits, and high-throughput chemical/genomic screens — combining large-scale unbiased discovery with precise circuit manipulation in the intact brain.
Jin-Quan Yu, PhD: The Yu lab develops new chemical reactions based on C-H activation — a way of directly transforming carbon-hydrogen bonds, which are normally unreactive, into new carbon-carbon or carbon-heteroatom bonds. Working from simple, abundant starting materials like aliphatic acids, amines, and alcohols, they design reactions that dramatically shorten the number of steps needed to synthesize drug molecules and other biologically active compounds. Their long-term aim is to make catalytic chemistry rival the precision and efficiency of natural enzymes. Core research areas include C-H activation itself, sustainable and asymmetric catalysis, and applying these methods to real synthetic problems, often in collaboration with computational chemists and pharmaceutical/agrochemical partners — training students in organometallic chemistry, catalyst design, and organic synthesis along the way.
Meng Zhang, PhD: The Zhang lab studies how cells organize themselves, interact with neighbors, and maintain balance within their natural tissue environments — and how these processes go wrong in aging and disease. To do this, they develop and apply spatial multi-omics tools: high-resolution, genome-scale profiling technologies that let them map individual cells' molecular states and interactions directly within tissue, preserving spatial and temporal context. The long-term goal is to translate these detailed cellular maps into a deeper molecular understanding of biology that can advance precision medicine, new disease treatments, and cell-based therapies.
Qinghai Zhang, PhD: The Zhang lab studies the chemical and structural biology of membrane proteins — a class of proteins that make up about a third of human genes and more than half of all human drug targets. The lab develops new methods and chemical tools to characterize how these proteins are structured and how they function, with particular interest in how membrane proteins interact with the surrounding lipids that govern their stability and activity. They work on discovering small-molecule drugs that target medically important membrane proteins such as transporters, GPCRs, and ion channels, including solving their structures to understand how drugs bind and act. The lab also develops new synthetic chemistry methods to build biologically relevant molecules for these studies.
Jiang Zhu, PhD: The Zhu lab combines computational modeling with experimental validation to tackle problems in disease prevention and therapeutics, spanning three main areas. In antibody discovery and vaccine design, they build next-generation sequencing and computational tools to identify functional antibodies against viruses like HIV-1, RSV, and Zika, track how broadly neutralizing antibodies develop during infection, and use structural modeling to design new vaccine components (immunogens). In optical control of neural circuits, they engineer light-sensitive proteins to precisely control ion channels and signaling pathways relevant to neurodegenerative disease. In structure-function studies, they build computational tools that use cryo-electron microscopy data to construct atomic-level models of large molecular machines like viruses, enzymes, and channels.
